content:
Reports yesterday claimed that Apple had previously considered designing an exclusive version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, before ultimately deciding to shelve the plan.

The Bloomberg report cited three reasons behind Apple's decision, one of which was a reluctance to contradict the stance taken by Steve Jobs when he launched the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the decisive factor…

On the surface, designing a shorter Apple Pencil to pair with the iPhone Ultra is an appealing concept. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same functionality seems entirely reasonable.

Samsung launched the Galaxy Note phablet in 2011 with an S-Pen stylus. The idea at the time was that the device could to some extent replace a paper notebook, and that design lasted for a decade, with a loyal following, before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman listed three reasons why Apple ultimately abandoned the idea:

  • Putting the Pencil on the side of the device rather than the top would make it awkward to hold
  • It would contradict Steve's view that a stylus is a poor substitute for a finger
  • It would leave unsightly marks on the screen

I don't think the first reason would be the main consideration, because mounting it on the top of the device would also have been a viable option. This would require a very short stylus, admittedly, but I think it would still be acceptable.

I also have reservations about the second reason. What Steve objected to at the time was not the idea that a smartphone could use a stylus, but that every model had to rely on one. Making the iPhone easy to operate with a finger was the real breakthrough.

In any case, Steve was also famously reluctant to adopt touch screens on the Mac on the grounds of poor ergonomics, yet we still expect the upcoming MacBook Pro model to include this feature, showing that Apple is not afraid to overturn the positions once held by its co-founder.

I believe the third factor is the one that truly killed the idea. The surface of a foldable screen is necessarily thinner and more flexible than that of existing devices. Apple is reportedly waiting a long time for its first foldable iPhone precisely because of concerns about the screen's appearance and durability; if an Apple Pencil were to rub against it on a regular basis, both would suffer.

If Apple ultimately manages to solve this problem, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed for a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
